snippets.output: A 51-year-old man’s consumption of 3–5 drinks of scotch per night, including before working on his car, suggests alcohol-induced hand tremors.
Alcohol-induced hand tremors are also known as alcoholic tremors or alcohol-induced parkinsonism.

For this 51-year-old man with an action tremor during activities such as pouring drinks, pointing a remote, and working on his car, the most appropriate treatment for the tremor would be to reduce or stop alcohol consumption.

For the 51-year-old man with an action tremor that occurs during activities such as pouring drinks, pointing a remote, and working on his car, participation in Alcoholics Anonymous and counseling to address alcohol use disorder are the most appropriate treatments for the tremor.
Aripiprazole is an antipsychotic medication primarily used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and it is not used to treat alcohol-induced tremors.
Carbidopa is used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease and is not used to treat alcohol-induced tremors.
Phenobarbital is a barbiturate used to treat seizures and insomnia, but it is not used to treat alcohol-induced tremors.
Propranolol is a beta-blocker used to treat high blood pressure and other cardiovascular conditions, but it is not used to treat alcohol-induced tremors.

A 51-year-old man's tremor is likely exacerbated by his alcohol consumption, so addressing alcohol use as an underlying contributor is crucial to managing his symptoms, and referral to Alcoholics Anonymous would be an essential part of his treatment plan.
